transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-10-27 16:00 UTC
- Duration: 48 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Riya (Redwood SE), Ethan (Redwood DevAdv), Alex (FastPass Eng Lead), Maya (PM), Samir (Platform), Lina (Security)

Topics: quickstart SDKs (Py/TS), auth and environment variables, sandbox provisioning, hosted vs dedicated cost/latency, security requirements (SOC2, KMS, SSO)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on the account, with Riya our SE and Ethan who helps with quickstarts. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Alex: Good, thanks. Excited to see the SDK flow — we want to move fast, we've got a small POC timeline, uh, about 4 weeks ideally.
[00:20] Maya: Yes, and our main asks are low latency for inference in the product, and no customer data leaving our VPC unless encrypted and audited.
[00:30] Jordan: Great, that's exactly what we'll cover. We'll walk through the Python and TypeScript quickstarts, auth options, and share the sandbox links. Riya, do you want to start the demo?
[00:40] Riya: Sure. I'm going to share my screen — starting at the Redwood Console home, you can see the model catalog. For the quickstart repo we typically show a small express app and a Flask example. Note: the console sometimes shows "Redwood consol" in the UI title in our test build, ignore that.
[01:05] Riya: First auth pattern: API key environment var. You drop REDWOOD_API_KEY into your .env, or use Secrets Manager. Example in Python: client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')). Then you can call .generate or .chat.
[01:30] Samir: Quick question — do keys support scope (read-only vs write) and TTL? We want short-lived creds for the product.
[01:38] Riya: Yes, we have scoped keys and can mint short-lived tokens via the Private control plane; for Hosted keys default are long-lived but you can rotate and use one-time tokens through the SDK. There's also SSO integration for team users and service accounts.
[01:55] Lina: From security, do you integrate with KMS for customer-managed keys or HSM?
[02:02] Ethan: Yep, Private deployments support KMS/HSM — you can bring your own KMS in the VPC package. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption with Redwood-managed keys, and an enterprise add-on for CMKs.
[02:20] Jordan: We're noting that — Lina we'll send the security pack link after this.
[02:28] Alex: Nice. On the SDK — what's the diff between the Node and Python SDK? Performance wise?
[02:36] Riya: Functionality parity is close; the Node SDK has streaming helpers that integrate with websockets and client-side streams, Python uses a streaming iterator. Under the hood both call the same HTTP API. There might be small differences in error handling — the snippets in the repo show both.
[02:55] Riya: I'm going to run the quickstart locally. First step is pip install redwood-sdk and npm i @redwood/sdk (or similar). Then set REDWOOD_API_KEY in a .env, start the Flask app, and hit /generate.
[03:20] [screen noise/typing sounds]
[03:30] Riya: Here's the generate call response — you can see tokens, latency ms, and model metadata. This output includes a token breakdown — the Console shows token-level cost too.
[03:48] Alex: Are those token numbers accurate for our billing? We need predictable unit economics.
[03:55] Jordan: Yes, the hosted API charges per token. For Dedicated you can get committed throughput + flat unit cost; Redwood Optimize also gives recommendations on batching and quant profiles to reduce cost.
[04:10] Maya: Can you explain batching vs latency tradeoff? We have a p95 latency SLO of 200ms for single-turn queries.
[04:20] Riya: Sure — batching groups requests for GPU throughput. If your QPS is low, batching hurts latency; if high, it helps cost per token. We configure continuous batching with latency thresholds in Redwood Dedicated. For p95=200ms single-turn, Hosted low-latency variants or Dedicated with small batch window is best.
[04:45] Samir: If we pick Dedicated, what's the autoscale and burst model? We have spiky traffic.
[04:51] Jordan: Dedicated pools support autoscaling and burst credits; you can configure a baseline and burst to handle spikes. We'll include recommended pool sizes based on your expected qps.
[05:05] Alex: Ok. Now, on env setup: we have CI where secrets are stored in our vault, and we deploy containers to ECS behind a proxy. Any gotchas?
[05:15] Ethan: For ECS you'll want to set the REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var from your vault, and if you're inside a VPC using Private, you'll configure peering or private endpoints. One common gotcha: ensure egress rules allow connections to the Redwood control plane, or if using Private on-prem, the control plane can be configured to be customer-managed.
[05:40] [crosstalk]
[05:45] Riya: Also, for on-prem or air-gapped we provide an installer image — it's a bit more involved but we can hand off the ops runbook.
[05:55] Maya: Can you show the quickstart repo structure?
[06:00] Riya: Yep — repo has /python_quickstart, /node_quickstart, and /examples. The env.example shows REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_MODEL (model id), REDWOOD_REGION. For Private clients we sometimes add REDWOOD_VPC_ENDPOINT.
[06:20] Riya: Example TS snippet: const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY, region: process.env.REDWOOD_REGION }); const resp = await client.chat.create({ model: 'redwood-large-001', messages: [...] });
[06:40] Alex: If we wanted to stream directly to the browser, any additional auth pattern?
[06:45] Riya: We recommend short-lived tokens minted by your backend for browser clients. Backend calls Redwood with the service key and mints a session token with a TTL. The browser uses that token to open a websocket to the stream endpoint.
[07:05] Samir: Is there an example for minting tokens in the repo?
[07:09] Riya: Yes, there's a small Node snippet — we will point you to it.
[07:15] Jordan: Quick qualification — what's your timeline again? Four weeks you said? Any procurement or security gate that would push it further out?
[07:25] Maya: Procurement needs a SOC2 report and our legal needs standard DPA reviewed. Security needs KMS integration details.
[07:33] Lina: Also audit logs and RD access controls — we need RBAC for team members.
[07:40] Ethan: We support audit logs and SSO (SAML/SCIM) for user access, and RBAC for token scopes. SOC2 report is in the enterprise pack; we'll share a link.
[07:52] Alex: Regarding performance — we want to run a quick bench with 1k sample prompts. Can we run that on Hosted first?
[07:58] Riya: Yes, Hosted is easiest to benchmark. If you hit capacity limits we'll recommend Dedicated. For your dataset we can run a sample bench and return p50/p95/p99 and token costs.
[08:12] Jordan: Let's plan to run the bench once Samir shares the sample prompt set and the typical request shapes.
[08:20] Samir: I'll share that by end of week. Also, how are partial responses and timeouts handled? We saw incomplete responses with another vendor and want guaranteed fallback.
[08:30] Riya: The SDK surfaces streaming and non-streaming — if a model times out, Redwood has automatic retry policies and fallback routing to lower-capacity models or cached responses; you can configure graceful degradation in the Console.
[08:45] Alex: Great. Any limitations around token limits? We're looking at longer context windows (20k tokens).
[08:52] Riya: We support several model families and up to 32k contexts for some variants; the model catalog shows the max seq. Keep in mind larger context increases memory usage and cost.
[09:05] [short pause]
[09:12] Maya: Can we talk about data retention? We need cert that customer PII isn't used to train models.
[09:18] Ethan: For Hosted, by default we don't train on customer data for enterprise customers; there's an explicit opt-in. Private deployments never share data. We'll include the data handling section in the security pack.
[09:32] Lina: Do you provide per-tenant encryption keys?
[09:35] Riya: With Private you can bring your own KMS and have CMKs per tenant; Hosted enterprise has options for customer-managed keys as an add-on.
[09:46] Alex: Ok — switching back to quickstart details: in CI how do we test prompts and run evals?
[09:54] Riya: We recommend using Redwood Optimize — you can push prompt sets and get quality regression alerts. There's also a local eval harness in the repo that runs test prompts and asserts outputs.
[10:10] Jordan: I'll put the Optimize docs link in the follow-up.
[10:14] Maya: On the pricing side, can you share an example cost calc for our expected volume?
[10:19] Jordan: We'll send a sample TCO: hosted per-token plus embedding costs; Dedicated has a baseline monthly and lower per-token rates. We'll include an example using your QPS and average token lengths.
[10:35] Alex: Any known gotchas when migrating from another vendor? We had issues with KV cache rehydration and session state.
[10:43] Riya: Ah yes — KV cache differences can be tricky. Redwood manages KV cache and allows you to persist session cache; there are examples showing how to checkpoint and restore KV. Sometimes transcripts show 'KV cash' in automatic transcripts, lol.
[10:58] Samir: Ha. Good. One last technical: do you support on-the-fly quantization profiles? We want to try q4/8 for cost.
[11:06] Riya: Yes, Optimize recommends quant profiles based on your workload. Dedicated runtime supports relaxed precision kernels and quantized models. We'll include suggested profiles in the follow-up.
[11:20] [longer typing/screen share as Riya walks repo]
[11:55] Riya: Sharing the quickstart link now: https://github.com/redwood-ai/quickstarts (note: placeholder link), and the security pack: https://redwood.example.com/security/fastpass. We'll actually send the real links in the follow-up.
[12:15] Alex: Cool. For the sandbox, what's needed from our side to grant access?
[12:20] Jordan: Just an email list for devs you want seeded in the sandbox and any IP allowlist if you want to restrict to your corp IPs. If Private, Samir will need to coordinate VPC peering info.
[12:34] Maya: Sounds good.
[12:36] Jordan: Ok, recap — action items: Jordan sends pricing and Dedicated vs Hosted comparison, Riya posts quickstart artifacts and short-lived token examples, Samir sends VPC/CIDR and prompt set, Maya to assemble success criteria doc. We'll schedule the perf bench the week of Nov 10.
[12:58] Alex: That works. Thanks everyone.
[13:02] Jordan: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the links and a calendar invite for the bench.

End transcript.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-hear (e.g., "KV cash"), speaker attribution sometimes generic in automated exports. Some crosstalk and filler words preserved.
